helpMsg:
ASCII art drawings are rendered as SVG images. This variant uses a fence of many backticks. The shorter form is a code block with the language ascii (see lia-ascii). The fence must not be indented.

Examples:

  `````````````````````````````````
                           .--->  F
  A       B     C   D     /
  *-------*-----*---*----*----->  E
           \            ^ \
            v          /   '--->  G
             B --> C -'
  `````````````````````````````````

A code block with the language ascii is rendered as an SVG image (svgbob). The fence must start at the left margin, an indented block is shown as plain code.

Drawing vocabulary:
  - _ |  \ /       lines
  +                 square corner
  . , ' `           rounded corners
  * # o O           dots, also as arrow ends
  < > ^ v V A       arrow heads
  Unicode box-drawing characters and emojis are also allowed.

Example:
  ``` ascii
  +------+   +-----+
  | Foo  +-->| Bar |
  +------+   +--+--+
                |
                v
          .-----------.
          |  rounded  |
          '-----------'
  ```

Text after the language ascii (on the same line as the opening fence) is shown as a caption below the image. It can contain Markdown.

Example:
  ``` ascii  Fig.: A __simple__ box
  +-----+
  | Box |
  +-----+
  ```

Text in double quotes inside an ASCII drawing is not drawn, but rendered as LiaScript on top of the image: Markdown, formulas, animations, quizzes, ... Lines whose quotes start at the same column form one multi-line block. The placement is not pixel-precise, so adjust the quotes and the frame by hand.

Example:
  ``` ascii
  +-------------------------------------------+
  | "$ \sum_{i=1}^n i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} $"   |
  +-------------------------------------------+
  | "Gauss found this at the age of __9__."   |
  +-------------------------------------------+
  ```
Inline `code` has `back-ticks around` it.

To insert a code block with syntax highlight, enclose your code snippet with three back-ticks (```) that is followed by a language code. To search all language codes, visit the link below, but in most cases you can simply add either the name of the language or the typical file-ending.

Examples:

  ```javascript
  var s = "JavaScript syntax highlighting";
  alert(s);
  s;
  ```

  ```python
  s = "Python syntax highlighting"
  print(s)
  ```

  ```
  No language indicated, so no syntax highlighting.
  But let's throw in a <b>tag</b>.
  ```

You can name your snippets by adding just after the language code. At default, it will be visible, but by adding a plus (+) in front of your filename you can make this more expressible, whereby a minus (-) will hide it at first. In this way you can also group multiple files into a (executable) project.

Examples:

  ```javascript    Visible.js
  alert("Visible JavaScript file");
  ```

  ```javascript   +Visible.js
  alert("Also visible JavaScript file");
  ```

  ```javascript   -Hidden.js
  alert("Hidden JavaScript file on init");
  ```

helpMsg:
Default output: a code block with @output after the language is not shown as code, its content is shown in the terminal of an executable project when the slide loads. It is replaced by the real result after the first execution. This is useful for courses that are read offline or on GitHub, where nothing can be executed. The @output block has to be the last block of the project. A plus (+) shows the content as normal output (stdout), a minus (-) as an error (stderr).

Example:

  ``` js     -EvalScript.js
  let str = "hello world";

  consolelog(str)
  ```
  ``` text    -@output
  There is an error in line 3 ...
  ```
  <script>@input</script>

Executable code with asynchronous results. End the script with "LIA: wait", so that LiaScript keeps the code block in the running state. Send output later with send.lia(...) or console.log(...) and finish with send.lia("LIA: stop").

Useful control strings and functions:
  "LIA: wait"                  keep running (async)
  "LIA: stop"                  finish the execution
  "LIA: clear"                 clear the terminal
  send.lia("text")             print output and keep running
  send.lia("text", [], true)   print as success
  send.lia("text", [], false)  print as error
  send.liascript("## md")      render LiaScript in the output
  send.lia("HTML: <b>x</b>")   render raw HTML in the output
  console.log/warn/error/debug(...)

Example:
  ```js
  let i = 0
  const id = setInterval(() => console.log(i++), 500)
  setTimeout(() => { clearInterval(id); send.lia("LIA: stop") }, 3000)
  ```
  <script>
    eval(`@input`)
    "LIA: wait"
  </script>

                                  highlight a range, repeatable with ;
                                  color: error, log, warn, debug, info

                                  type:  fullLine (default), text,
                                         screenLine
  data-tabSize, data-fontSize, data-firstLineNumber

Example:
  <!-- data-theme="chaos" data-marker="1 0 1 12 warn;" -->
  ```js
  let a = 1
  a = a + 1
  ```

helpMsg:
Narration comments: the paragraph below --{{n}}-- is read out loud by the text-to-speech engine when animation step n is reached. Only one paragraph is allowed per comment, Markdown can be used inside.

In Presentation mode the text is spoken and hidden, in Slides mode it is spoken and shown in a side panel, and in Textbook mode it is shown in place. A comment never reveals anything on the slide by itself, so pair it with a {{n}} block for the same step (see lia-effect-presentation). Several comments with the same number are read one after another.
The default voice is defined within the main header, if not english will be used. This main voice can be changed per section by adding a section comment.

Example:
  <!--
  author:   ...
  email:    ...
  ...
  narrator: UK English Female
  -->

  # Title

               --{{0}}--
  I will speak with a female *UK* accent.

  ## Section
  <!-- narrator: US English Male -->

               --{{0}}--
  This entire section will be spoken by an American man.

               --{{1}}--
  But only this section...

To simplify the voice-search, simply start typing "voice" and fuzzy search all responsive voice or click on the link below.

You can change the voice also per comment by adding it directly after the number of appearance.
Type "voice" for fuzzy searching all responsive voices or click on the link below.

Example:
        --{{0 Australian Female}}--
  I will speak with a female Australian accent,
  no matter what the default language is.

        --{{0 Deutsch Male}}--
  Und hier äußert sich gerade ein deutscher Mann.

If you want to speak out some additional text that shall not appear in the textbook mode, then simply put your comment into a HTML comment tag.

Example:
  <!-- --{{2}}--
  I will speak with the default voice, but not appear
  elsewhere within the document.
  -->
replace: <!-- --{{${1:number}}}-- ${2:Enter some **text** that gets read out aloud!} -->

helpMsg:
If you want to speak out some additional text that shall not appear in the textbook mode and speak with another voice, then simply put your comment with a voice definition into a HTML comment tag.

Example:
  <!-- --{{2 Deutsch Female}}--
  I will speak with a German voice, but not appear
  elsewhere within the document.
  -->

Type "voice" for fuzzy searching or click on the link below for more information.
replace: <!-- --{{${1:number} ${2:voice}}}-- ${3:Enter some **text** that gets read out aloud!} -->

helpMsg:
Multimedia comment: attach an audio (or video) link at the end of a narration comment to play your own recording at this animation step instead of the text-to-speech voice. The file is only loaded and played when the step is reached in Presentation or Slides mode. It never shows up as a visible player. For a visible player, put the audio link outside of a comment.

Example:

  To play an audio file during your animation step,
  simply attach the link at the end of your comment.
  ?[⏯](recording/audio_1.mp3)

Example:

Bundle multiple blocks into one animation step by enclosing them in two lines of three or more asterisks (*). The effect definition goes above the opening line. Alternatively, use a <section> ... </section> wrapper instead of the asterisks (see lia-effect-section).
The entire block can also be styled and the animation tweaked, but the required comment tag has to be defined before the Markdown block. Animate.css is included at default.

Examples:
                    {{1}}
  *************************************************

  Both blocks will appear at once. Nesting of other
  {2}{inline} and block effects is also allowed.


  | Also | with  |
  |------|-------|
  | any  | table |

  **************************************************

A slide that works as a presentation and as a textbook: every visible step {{n}} is paired with a narration --{{n}}-- for the same step. Think of {{n}} as the bullet point and --{{n}}-- as the speaker notes for it.

How the narration is shown depends on the mode:
  Presentation -> spoken, text hidden
  Slides       -> spoken, text shown in the side panel
  Textbook     -> not spoken, text shown in place

A --{{n}}-- comment alone never reveals anything on the slide, so always pair it with a {{n}} block. Step 0 introduces the slide.

Example:
  ## Photosynthesis

               --{{0}}--
  Plants turn light into sugar. Let us look at the inputs.

                 {{1}}
  * Light, water and CO2 go in

               --{{1}}--
  Three things are needed: light, water and carbon dioxide.

Examples:

Example:

Including audio is done with a starting question mark (?) that is followed a common Markdown link. If you want to include soundcloud, then you only have to refer to the link and the player gets embedded into your course.

Example:

  ?[singing birds](https://bigsoundbank.com/UPLOAD/mp3/1068.mp3)

  ?[soundcloud](https://soundcloud.com/glennmorrison/beethoven-moonlight-sonata)

An optional information can be attached to every audio file by adding double quotes after the link in the parentheses. This will be attached as a subtitle to this element and can also include Markdown syntax.

Example:

  ?[singing birds](https://bigsoundbank.com/UPLOAD/mp3/1068.mp3 "optional infos")

Optional information can be attached to every video by adding double quotes after the link in the parentheses. This will be attached as a subtitle to this element and can also include Markdown syntax.

Example:

  !?[eLab](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bICfKRyKTwE "Some information about the previous __eLab__ project.")

Example:

Example:

Example:

A link with the text preview-lia to the raw URL of another LiaScript course is rendered as a preview card with the title, description, logo and author taken from the course header. Clicking the card opens the course.

Example:

Links with mailto: open the email program, links with tel: start a phone call on mobile devices.

Example:

Two-column layout: an image followed directly by text (no blank line between them) forms one paragraph. The image floats to the left with up to 50% of the width and the text flows beside it. A blank line between image and text puts the text below the image instead.

Example:
  ![A lion](img/lion.jpg "The king of the jungle")
  Lions live in groups called prides. This text is shown
  to the right of the image.

Inline Footnotes are composed of a reference in brackets with a starting caret. The following text has to be put into parentheses, only one line is allowed.

   Example with [^1](inline _footnote_) and some more text.

Multiline footnotes have to be split into a reference and into a comment. Footnote references are defined by brackets with a starting caret and can appear everywhere within the text. Footnote texts have to be put at the end of the same section, because LiaScript parses every slide on its own. The id can be a number, a word or even an emoji.

Example:

Here is a footnote reference, [^1] and another.[^longnote]

...

[^1]: Here is the footnote text.

[^longnote]: Here's one with multiple blocks.

               Subsequent paragraphs are indented to show that they
               belong to the previous footnote.

Multiline footnotes have to be split into a reference and into a comment. Footnote texts start with a reference "tag", which is followed by a colon. They have to be put into the end of each section otherwise they are not interpreted as footnote texts and multi-block footnotes have to follow the previous indentation.
Example:
...

[^1]: Here is the footnote text.

[^longnote]: Here's one with multiple blocks.

               Subsequent paragraphs are indented to show that they
               belong to the previous footnote.

Define your own KaTeX macros in the main header (or a section header) with formula:. They can be used in every formula of the course. The line can be repeated for more macros.

Example:
  <!--
  formula: \R      \mathbb{R}
  formula: \norm   \left\lVert #1 \right\rVert
  -->

  # Main

  $ x \in \R $ and $ \norm{x} $

The main header is an HTML comment at the very top of the document. It defines the defaults of the course: authors, contact, version, language, the narrator voice, additional JavaScript and CSS, macros and more. Continuation lines have to be indented. Most settings can be overwritten per section (see lia-header-section).

Common fields:
  author      separate multiple authors with ;
  email       contact shown in the info panel
  version     0.x.x = development, nothing is stored;
              >= 1.0.0 = quiz, code and task states are stored
              (bump the major version when you move quizzes)
  language    UI language and typography (en, de, fr, es, ...)
  narrator    default text-to-speech voice (type "voice")
  comment     short description for the course card
  logo        image for the course card
  icon        replaces the default LiaScript icon
  mode        Presentation | Slides | Textbook
  repository  link to the source repository
  edit        true or a URL to edit the course online
  link        additional CSS files, one per line
  script      additional JavaScript files, one per line
  import      macros of other courses/templates
  translation link to a translated version

Type "lia-macro-" to find snippets for single header fields.

Example:
  <!--
  author:   Your Name
  email:    your@email.com
  version:  0.1.0
  language: en
  narrator: US English Female

  comment:  A short description of your course.
            Multiline is also okay.

  logo:     ./img/logo.png

  link:     https://cdn.example.com/library.css
  script:   https://cdn.example.com/library.js

  translation: Deutsch  translations/German.md
  -->

  # Course Title

### A Textquiz

### Multiple Choice

Just add as many points as you wish:

    [[X]] ...

### Single Choice

Just add as many points as you wish:

    [( )] ...
    [(X)] <-- Only the **X** is correct.
    [( )] ...

helpMsg:
Surveys use the quiz brackets but have no correct answer, only a submit button. Three or more underscores in double brackets create a one-line text input.

In a live classroom session, the answers of one-line inputs are shown as a word cloud, where comma-separated terms are counted. Use it for keywords or short phrases.

Example:
  Which programming languages do you know? Separate them with commas.

      [[___]]

A multi-line text survey (textarea). Every group of underscores separated by a space adds one row. The number of groups sets the number of rows, the length of a group does not matter. One pair of double brackets always creates exactly one input field. For several fields, write several surveys, each with its own question above it.

In a live classroom session, the answers of a textarea are listed one below the other, which suits longer answers.

Example:
  A two-line text survey:

      [[___ ___]]

  Please describe your opinion in a few sentences:

      [[___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___]]

Single-choice survey: like a single-choice quiz, but the parentheses contain an identifier instead of an X. Numeric identifiers let the classroom view plot the results as a distribution, while text identifiers are shown as categories. Identifiers do not have to be ordered or sequential.

Example:

  Choose between different options:

    [(1)] option 1
    [(2)] option 2
    [(0)] option 3

  What is your favorite color:

    [(red)]   red?
    [(blue)]  blue?
    [(green)] green?

Multiple-choice survey: like a multiple-choice quiz, but the brackets contain an identifier instead of an X. Start an identifier with a number (e.g. [[1 red]]) to get a numeric instead of a categorical representation in the classroom view.

Example:

  Choose as many options as your want:

    [[1]] option 1
    [[2]] option 2
    [[0]] option 0

  Mark all colors you like:

    [[red]]   red?
    [[blue]]  blue?
    [[green]] green?
    [[none]]  None of these ...

Single-choice matrix survey: the header contains the column identifiers in parentheses, every following row ([ ] + text) becomes its own single-choice question. Identifiers can be numbers or words.

Example:

  Give marks:

      [(-1)(0)(1)]
      [          ] LiaScript is great?
      [          ] I would use it to make online **courses**?
      [          ] I would use it for online **surveys**?

  What is your opinion:

      [(agree)(unsure)(maybe not so)]
      [                             ] LiaScript is great?
      [                             ] I would use it to make online **courses**?
      [                             ] I would use it for online **surveys**?

Multiple-choice matrix survey: the header contains the column identifiers in brackets, every following row ([ ] + text) becomes its own multiple-choice question. Identifiers can be numbers or words.

Example:

  Give marks:

      [[-1][0][1]]
      [          ] LiaScript is great?
      [          ] I would use it to make online **courses**?
      [          ] I would use it for online **surveys**?

  What is your opinion:

      [[agree][unsure][maybe not so]]
      [                             ] LiaScript is great?
      [                             ] I would use it to make online **courses**?
      [                             ] I would use it for online **surveys**?

You can enforce the visualization of a certain type, even if the structure of your table might look different.
Currently available data-types are (case-insensitive): lineplot (line), scatterplot (scatter), barchart (bar), boxplot, radar, piechart (pie), funnel, map, heatmap, parallel, graph, sankey, and none
If you do not want to show tables as diagrams, you can also use data-type="None" and only the table will be visible.

Example:
  <!-- data-type="pie" -->
  | Year | Finland | USA | Germany |   China |
  | ---- | -------:| ---:| -------:| -------:|
  | 1995 | 6.80942 |     | 4.42079 | 1.84192 |
  | 1996 | 6.86052 |     | 4.48319 | 1.85338 |
  | ...  |     ... | ... |     ... |     ... |

If the first column contains (not repeating) numbers as well as the other columns, lineplots are used as the default representation, a special tag is not required. If this isn't the case, then you can apply this tag to enforce the visualization as a lineplot.

Example:
  <!-- data-type="lineplot" -->
  | x's |  some y's  |    dist |
  | --- |:----------:| -------:|
  | 1   |    1 $    | 16 $km$ |
  | 2.2 |    2 $    | 12 $km$ |
  | 3.3 |    5 $    |  1 $km$ |
  | 4   | -12.333 $ |         |

If the first column contains repetitive numbers, scatterplots are used as the default representation if further numbers are determine, a special tag is not required.

Example:
  <!-- data-type="scatterplot" -->
  | x's |  some y's  |                              dist |
  | --- |:----------:| ---------------------------------:|
  | 1   |    1 $    |                           16 $km$ |
  | 2.2 |    2 $    |                           12 $km$ |
  | 3.3 |    5 $    |                            1 $km$ |
  | 4   | -12.333 $ | -555$km$ <-- this will be ignored |
  | 4   |            |                                 1 |

In contrast to a line or a scatter plot, if the first colum contains at least one entry thant cannot be parsed as a number, this might be represented also as BarChart. Which works perfectly with the following example. If the maximum values of the columns do not differ to much, then this dataset it represented as a BarChart, otherwise you might end up seeing only one huge bar, while the other bars are indistiguishable from each other. In this case other visualization are chosen.

Example:
  <!-- data-type="barchart" -->
  | Animal          | weight in kg | Lifespan years | Mitogen |
  | --------------- | ------------:| --------------:| -------:|
  | Mouse           |        0.028 |              2 |      95 |
  | Flying squirrel |        0.085 |             15 |      50 |
  | Brown bat       |        0.020 |             30 |      10 |
  | Sheep           |           90 |             12 |      95 |
  | Human           |           68 |             70 |      10 |

If you have a ScatterPlot like representation, but actually want to use this data as primary data for your BoxPlot, you can manually change the type of visualization to BoxPlot, simply by adding the follwing attribute to the head of your table, as it is shown in the snippet below. Columns are then treated as datasets and get visualized accordingly.

Example:
  <!-- data-type="boxplot" -->
  | Random |    I |  II |
  | ------:| ----:| ---:|
  |    5.0 |  1.0 |   5 |
  |    6.0 |  1.0 |   4 |
  |    7.0 |  1.0 |   5 |
  |    8.0 |  1.0 |   5 |
  |    9.0 |  1.0 |   4 |
  |   10.0 |  1.0 |   5 |
  |    5.0 | 10.0 |   7 |
  |    6.0 | 10.0 |   8 |
  |    7.0 | 10.0 |   7 |
  |    8.0 | 10.0 |   7 |
  |    9.0 | 10.0 |   8 |

A radar chart draws one polygon per row with one axis per column. It is useful if the columns have very different scales (e.g. weight in kg and lifespan in years), which would make a BarChart unreadable. Do not rely on the automatic detection, set the type explicitly. Use at least 3 numeric columns.

Example:
  <!-- data-type="radar" -->
  | Animal          | weight in kg | Lifespan years | Mitogen |
  | --------------- | ------------:| --------------:| -------:|
  | Mouse           |        0.028 |              2 |      95 |
  | Flying squirrel |        0.085 |             15 |      50 |
  | Brown bat       |        0.020 |             30 |      10 |

If you have a table with only one row full of numbers, this will be automatically presented as an pie chart. The head represents the categories and the body the quatities.

Example:
  | Classic | Country | Reggae | Hip-Hop | Hard-Rock | Samba |
  | -------:| -------:| ------:| -------:| ---------:| -----:|
  |      50 |      50 |    100 |     200 |       350 |   250 |

  <!-- data-type="PieChart" -->
  | Music-Style | Classic | Country | Reggae | Hip-Hop | Hard-Rock | Samba |
  |:----------- | -------:| -------:| ------:| -------:| ---------:| -----:|
  | 1994        |      50 |      50 |    100 |     200 |       350 |   250 |
  | 2014        |      20 |      30 |    100 |     220 |       400 |   230 |
  | demo 2034   |       5 |      12 |     98 |     293 |       345 |    32 |

A map is similar to a BarChart from the table structure, but if you want to depict your data on a real map, you will have to add a geojson-file, that contains all relevant data about the form of your countries, states, cities, etc. The first column has to match the names of your objects in your geojson data, that is attached to your table in the following way:

Example:
  <!-- data-type="map" data-src="https://code.highcharts.com/mapdata/custom/europe.geo.json" -->
  | Country                | percent |
  | ---------------------- | ------- |
  | Albania                | 73.5    |
  | Andorra                | 98.9    |
  | Armenia                | 72.4    |
  | ...                    |         |

Another type of visualization is a HeatMap, which is used, if the table head and the first column do only contain numbers, in other words coordinates. If you want to use categories instead of coordinate numbers, you can enforce the usage of a heatmap, with the comment shown below:

Example:
  <!--
  data-type="heatmap"
  data-title="Seattle mean temperature in Fahrenheit"
  data-show
  -->
    | Seattle |  Jan |  Feb |  Mar |  Apr |  May |  ... |
    | -------:| ----:| ----:| ----:| ----:| ----:| ----:|
    |       0 | 40.7 | 41.5 | 43.6 | 46.6 | 51.4 |  ... |
    |       2 |  ... |  ... |  ... |  ... |  ... |  ... |

A parallel coordinates plot draws one vertical axis per column and one line per row. It is useful if there are too many categories for a readable BarChart. Do not rely on the automatic detection, set the type explicitly.

Example:
  <!-- data-type="parallel" -->
  | Country                | GDP growth (%) | Births per woman | Life expectancy ...
  | ---------------------- | --------------:| ----------------:| -------------------
  | Albania                |            7.5 |            1.858 |               76.63
  | Andorra                |          3.570 |            1.260 |                 NaN
  | Austria                |          2.178 |            1.414 |               80.44
  | ...                    |            ... |              ... |                 ...

If the first column and the head of the table are equal, then the interpreter tries to interpret the content of the table as an adjacency matrix, which defines a graph. If those values are symetrical according to the diagonal, then the matrix defines an "undirected graph".
In contrast to this, if those values differ, then the result is simply an an "directed graph", whereby the values define the strength of the line.

Example:
  <!-- data-title="Undirected Graph" -->
  | Graph |  A  |  B  |  C  |  D  |  E  |
  |:----- |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
  | A     |  0  |  1  |  0  |  1  |  0  |
  | B     |  1  |  0  |  0  |  1  |  0  |
  | C     |  0  |  0  |  0  |  0  |  0  |
  | D     |  1  |  1  |  0  |  0  |  1  |
  | E     |  0  |  0  |  0  |  1  |  0  |

  <!-- data-title="Directed Graph" -->
  | Graph |  A  |  B  |  C  |  D  |  E  |
  |:----- |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
  | A     |  0  | 12  |  0  |  1  |  0  |
  | B     | -22 |  0  |  0  | 0.4 |  0  |
  | C     |  0  |  0  |  0  |  0  |  0  |
  | D     |  2  | 12  |  0  |  0  |  1  |
  | E     |  0  |  0  |  0  |  2  |  0  |

A Sankey diagram is a special type of directed graph that can be used to streams or the flow of something, such as engergy, money, etc.

Example:
  <!-- data-type="sankey" -->
  | Sankey |  A  |  B  |  C  |  D  |  E  |
  |:------ |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
  | A      |     |  2  |     |     |     |
  | B      |  3  |     |     |     |     |
  | C      |  1  |  1  |     |     |     |
  | D      |     |  1  |  1  |     |     |
  | E      |  2  |  1  |  1  |  1  |     |

Simply data-type="none" to prevent any kind of visualization.

Example:
  <!-- data-type="none" -->
  | Sankey |  A  |  B  |  C  |  D  |  E  |
  |:------ |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
  | A      |     |  2  |     |     |     |
  | B      |  3  |     |     |     |     |
  | C      |  1  |  1  |     |     |     |
  | D      |     |  1  |  1  |     |     |
  | E      |  2  |  1  |  1  |  1  |     |

Simply add this attribute or set it to true (data-show="true"), if you want to visualize your data immediately, without the need to click in the switch-button. It is still possible for your users to switch to the table representation.

Example:
  <!-- data-show -->
  | Sankey |  A  |  B  |  C  |  D  |  E  |
  |:------ |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
  | A      |     |  2  |     |     |     |
  | B      |  3  |     |     |     |     |
  | C      |  1  |  1  |     |     |     |
  | D      |     |  1  |  1  |     |     |
  | E      |  2  |  1  |  1  |  1  |     |

Like in the mathematical sense, set this attribute or set it to true (data-transpose="true"), if you want to switch rows and columns. One benefit is, that you can for example use PieChart and let your table grow vertically instead of using a horizontal monster.

Example:
  <!-- data-transpose -->
  | Music-Style {0-1}{1994} {1}{2014} |      Student rating |
  |:--------------------------------- | -------------------:|
  | Classic                           |   {0-1}{50} {1}{20} |
  | Country                           |   {0-1}{50} {1}{30} |
  | Reggae                            |                 100 |
  | Hip-Hop                           | {0-1}{200} {1}{220} |
  | Hard-Rock                         | {0-1}{350} {1}{400} |
  | Samba                             | {0-1}{250} {1}{230} |

Currently this attribute is used to refere to your geojson data, if you use the `data-type="Map"` representation, but this might change in the future to load and visualize data directly, such as csv.
If you are using geojson files from external websites such as: https://code.highcharts.com/mapdata/
It can be usefull to use anycors, if the data cannot be visualized due to CORS restrictions:

data-src="https://cors-anywhere.herokuapp.com/https://code.highcharts.com/mapdata/custom/europe.geo.json"

Example:
  <!-- data-type="map" data-src="https://code.highcharts.com/mapdata/custom/europe.geo.json" -->
  | Country                | percent |
  | ---------------------- | ------- |
  | Albania                | 73.5    |
  | Andorra                | 98.9    |
  | Armenia                | 72.4    |
  | ...                    |         |

A funnel (pyramid) chart uses the same table shape as a PieChart: a header with the categories and one row of numbers. It is never selected automatically.

Example:
  <!-- data-type="funnel" data-show -->
  | Visits | Sign-ups | Trials | Customers |
  | ------:| --------:| ------:| ---------:|
  |   1000 |      400 |    150 |        40 |

Sets the range of the x-axis. One side can be left empty to determine it automatically, e.g. data-xlim=",12".

Example:
  <!-- data-show data-xlim="1994,2000" -->
  | Year | Finland | Germany |
  | ---- | -------:| -------:|
  | 1995 |     6.8 |     4.4 |
  | 1996 |     6.9 |     4.5 |

Sets the range of the y-axis. One side can be left empty to determine it automatically, e.g. data-ylim="0,".

Example:
  <!-- data-show data-ylim="0,10" -->
  | Year | Finland | Germany |
  | ---- | -------:| -------:|
  | 1995 |     6.8 |     4.4 |
  | 1996 |     6.9 |     4.5 |

Flips a BarChart: the bars are drawn horizontally and the categories are listed on the y-axis. Useful for long category names.

Example:
  <!-- data-show data-orientation="horizontal" -->
  | Animal          | weight in kg | Lifespan years |
  | --------------- | ------------:| --------------:|
  | Mouse           |        0.028 |              2 |
  | Flying squirrel |        0.085 |             15 |

Tables can be sorted by clicking on a header cell. data-sortable="false" in the table comment turns this off for the whole table. It can also be set for single columns in a comment inside the header cell.

Example:
  <!-- data-sortable="false" -->
  | Rank | Name  |
  | ---- | ----- |
  | 1    | Alice |
  | 2    | Bob   |

A table that is shown as a diagram right away. All settings go into one HTML comment directly above the table:

  data-show            show the diagram instead of the table
  data-type            chart type (see lia-table-diagram-type)
  data-title           title of the diagram
  data-xlabel/ylabel   axis labels
  data-xlim/ylim       axis ranges, e.g. "0,10"
  data-transpose       swap rows and columns
  data-orientation     "horizontal" bars

Users can still switch between table and diagram.

Do not put another HTML comment directly above this one without a blank line, otherwise the table is shown as plain text.

data-xlabel="${3:year}"

| ${5:Year} | ${6:Finland} | ${7:Germany} |

helpMsg:
Task lists use the GitHub-flavoured Markdown syntax: a list item that starts with [ ] (open) or [X] (done). Users can check and uncheck the boxes. If the course version is 1.0.0 or higher, the states are stored persistently in the browser.

Example:
  - [ ] This is not checked by default
  - [X] This one is checked by default
  - [ ] Tasks can contain __Markdown__

Italic text, enclosed by single underscores. Equivalent to *text*.

Every emphasis span has to stay on one physical line. If the closing marker lands on the next line, stray markers will show up in the rendered text.

Example:
  This is _italic_ and this is _also **bold** inside_.

Italic text, enclosed by single asterisks. Equivalent to _text_.

Every emphasis span has to stay on one physical line.

Example:
  This is *italic* text.

Bold text, enclosed by double underscores. Equivalent to **text**.

Every emphasis span has to stay on one physical line.

Example:
  This is __bold__ and __bold with _italic_ inside__.

Bold text, enclosed by double asterisks. Equivalent to __text__.

Every emphasis span has to stay on one physical line.

Example:
  This is **bold** text.

Bold and italic text, enclosed by triple underscores. Equivalent to ***text***.

Example:
  This is ___bold and italic___.

Bold and italic text, enclosed by triple asterisks. Equivalent to ___text___.

Note: a line that contains only *** (three or more asterisks) is not text, it groups blocks for animations or marks a quiz solution.

Example:
  This is ***bold and italic***.

Strike-through text, enclosed by single tildes. This is a LiaScript extension.

Example:
  The price was ~20 €~ and is now 15 €.

Underlined text, enclosed by double tildes. This is a LiaScript extension, other Markdown viewers (e.g. GitHub) show it as strike-through.

Example:
  This is ~~underlined~~ text.

Strike-through and underlined text, enclosed by triple tildes. This is a LiaScript extension.

Example:
  This is ~~~struck and underlined~~~.

Superscript text, enclosed by carets. This is a LiaScript extension. For subscripts or more complex notation use a formula ($ x_i $).

Example:
  E = mc^2^ and the 1^st^ of May.

Text quiz: put the solution into double brackets and the user gets an input field. The answer is compared with the solution string. Text quizzes do not support a starting dash.

Example:
  What is the color of the sky?

      [[blue]]

If several answers should be accepted, add a script (lia-quiz-text-js) or use a selection (lia-quiz-select).

Selection quiz: a dropdown with options separated by `|`. The correct option is put into parentheses, and more than one option can be correct. Options may contain Markdown, images or formulas. Selections do not support a starting dash.

Example:
  What is the color of the sky?

      [[ red | (__blue__) | green | (black at night) ]]

  What is the derivative of $f(x) = x^6$?

      [[ $f'(x) = 6$ | ( $f'(x) = 6x^5$ ) | $f'(x) = 5x^6$ ]]

Gap text: text and selection quizzes can be placed inline, anywhere inside a paragraph, a list or a table. The width of the input field matches the length of the placeholder, so add spaces to make a gap wider. All gaps of one block are checked together.

Text around the brackets is ordinary text. To give hints, use [[?]] lines after the block.

Example:
  __I [[  have been learning  ]] English for seven years now.__

  The capital of France is [[ Paris ]] and of Italy [[ Rome ]].
  [[?]] Both are famous for their food.
replace: ${1:I} [[ ${2:have been learning} ]] ${3:English for seven years now.}

helpMsg:
Gap text with a dropdown: use the selection syntax inline. To accept several answers, put every acceptable option into parentheses.

Example:
  I [[ (have been learning) | ('ve been learning) | learned ]] English for seven years now.
replace: ${1:I} [[ (${2:have been learning}) | (${3:'ve been learning}) | ${4:learned} ]] ${5:English for seven years now.}

helpMsg:
Single-choice quiz (radio buttons): one line per option. [(X)] or [(x)] marks a correct option, [( )] a wrong one. If more than one option is marked, the user has to select only one of them. A starting dash (- [( )] ...) is allowed.

Example:
  This is a single choice quiz with three options:

      [( )] Add as many lines as you want.
      [(X)] The X marks the correct answer!
      [( )] This one is wrong.

Multiple-choice quiz (checkboxes): one line per option. [[X]] or [[x]] marks an option that has to be checked, [[ ]] one that has to stay unchecked. A starting dash (- [[ ]] ...) is allowed.

Example:
  This is a multiple choice quiz with four options:

      [[ ]] Add as many lines as you want.
      [[X]] The X marks the options that have to be checked!
      [[X]] There can be several of them.
      [[ ]] Empty brackets have to stay unchecked.

Matrix quiz: the first line holds the column labels. Every following row starts with [ and ends with ] followed by the row text. The cells of a row define its type: [ ] / [X] cells make a multiple-choice row, ( ) / (X) cells a single-choice row. All cells of one row must use the same type. Spacing is only cosmetic.

The brackets in the header are only labels. Use [...] or (...) so that you can put the other type of bracket into a label as text.

Example:
  - [[male (der)] (female [die]) [neuter (das)]]
  - [    [X]           [ ]             [ ]     ]  Mann - German for man
  - [    ( )           (X)             ( )     ]  Frau - German for woman

Hints can be added directly after any type of quiz, as many as you want. They are revealed one at a time when the user clicks the hint button. A starting dash (- [[?]] ...) is allowed.

Example:
  A text quiz with two hints:

      [[solution]]
      [[?]] This is the first hint
      [[?]] This is a second hint

  And a multiple choice quiz with one hint:

      [[X]] This is correct!
      [[ ]] This is wrong!
      [[?]] Click on the first option!

A solution block is shown after the quiz was solved or resolved. Enclose any Markdown blocks (text, images, code, ...) between two lines of three or more asterisks.

Important: there must not be a blank line between the last line of the quiz (answer, hint or script) and the opening asterisks. Otherwise the block is not recognized and the solution is visible all the time. Blank lines inside the block are fine.

Example:
  What is the color of the sky?

      [[blue]]
      [[?]] Look up!
      *************************************

      During the day the color is blue, if
      it is not cloudy.

      ![blue sky](./img/sunny.jpg)

      *************************************

key: complete quiz: question, hints, script, solution

helpMsg:
A script after a single-choice quiz can change how it is checked, e.g. to accept other answers or to count trials. @input is replaced by a number (unquoted):

  -1 -> nothing selected
   0 -> the first option
   1 -> the second option ...

The last expression has to be true (solved) or false (not solved).

Example:
      [( )] Check this ...
      [(X)] ... or this
      <script>
        let selected = @input;
        selected === 0 || selected === 1
      </script>
replace:
<script>
  // @input is replaced by the index of the selected option
  // (0 = first option, -1 = nothing selected)
  let selected = @input;

  ${1:selected === 1}
</script>

helpMsg:
A script after a multiple-choice quiz can change how it is checked, e.g. to let partially correct answers pass. @input is replaced by an array (unquoted) with one entry per option:

  1 -> checked
  0 -> unchecked

The last expression has to be true (solved) or false (not solved).

Example:
  Get at least one right ...

      [[ ]] Wrong.
      [[X]] Right.
      [[ ]] Wrong.
      [[X]] Right.
      <script>
        let checked = @input;
        (checked[1] === 1 || checked[3] === 1) &&
        checked[0] === 0 && checked[2] === 0
      </script>
replace:
<script>
  // @input is replaced by an array such as [0,1,0,1],
  // with 1 for a checked and 0 for an unchecked box
  let checked = @input;

  ${1:// accept every answer with at least one correct option
  checked[1] === 1 || checked[3] === 1}
</script>

helpMsg:
A generic script that can be attached directly after any quiz. Before it runs, @input is replaced as text, so its form depends on the quiz type:

  text / gap text  -> raw text, wrap it in backticks: `@input`
  single choice    -> number (-1 if nothing is selected)
  selection        -> number of the selected option
  multiple choice  -> array, e.g. [0,1,1] (1 = checked)
  matrix           -> nested array, e.g. [[1,0,0], 1]

The last expression has to be true (solved) or false (not solved).

Example:
      [[52]]
      <script>
        Number(`@input`) === 52
      </script>
replace:
<script>
  ${1:// @input is replaced by the current quiz input:
  // * text / gap text  -> raw text, use it as `@input`
  // * single choice    -> number (-1 if nothing selected)
  // * selection        -> number of the selected option
  // * multiple choice  -> array, e.g. [0,1,1] (1 = checked)
  // * matrix           -> nested array, one entry per row
  let input = @input;

  true; // return true if solved, otherwise false}
</script>

helpMsg:
Inserts a single-choice quiz with three options:

      [( )] This is wrong.
      [(X)] The correct option.
      [( )] Still not right.

Inserts a multiple-choice quiz with four options:

      [[ ]] Add as many options as you want.
      [[X]] The X marks the correct answer!
      [[ ]] ... this is wrong ...
      [[X]] ... this has to be checked too ...

Generic quiz: [[!]] has no input element of its own. The quiz is solved if the script evaluates to true and not solved if it evaluates to false. Use it for checks that do not fit the other quiz types, e.g. to test the state of an interactive element or the result of a code block.

Use alert(...) to inspect values while developing.

Example:
  Only lucky people can solve this quiz:

      [[!]]
      <script>
